I honestly hadn't heard about this so I decided to look into it, and you couldn't be more wrong.

I just went and read the wikipedia page, 5 different news articles, and watched 3 different sets of footage multiple times, and It's pretty fucking clear that Oscar Grant was restrained and not a threat even if he was resisting at that point. However three eyewitnesses of the account testified that neither Grant nor the other suspects actively resisted the officers at any time, and each of the witnesses expressed disgust at the behavior from officers preceding the shooting that night.

The point is even if Grant was resisting, there was zero justification for the use of lethal force from Officer Johannes Mehserle, who was armed with a Taser and was wearing it on the left side of his body (on the opposite side from which he wore his gun). Although several experts who observed video evidence suggested Mehserle might have confused his gun for his Taser causing him to mistakenly believe he was tasering Grant. The prosecution argued that modern Tasers weigh half as much as handguns, and that the position of Mehserle's Taser "in relation to his duty weapon, combined with the different 'feel' and color of the two weapons made it highly unlikely that he would have mistaken one for the other.

Whether Mehserle was a cold-blooded executioner or he was simply an incompetent man incapable of handling the pressure who lost control and panicked, I honestly don't know. What I do know is that in either case Mehserle should never have been issued a uniform or placed in a position of authority.

The jury found Mehserle guilty of involuntary manslaughter, and not guilty of both the second-degree murder and voluntary manslaughter charges. The jury also found Mehserle guilty of a gun enhancement charge that could have added up to ten years to his prison sentence, made him ineligible for probation, and forced him to serve 85 percent of his sentence as opposed to the 50 percent that most state prisoners serve.

The judge overturned the gun enhancement, which could have added 3 to 10 years to the sentence, and in the end he was sentenced to a mere two years with double credit for time already served (due to CA jail/prison overcrowding, one day in custody counts as two for most inmates), reducing his term by 292 days for the 146 days he has already spent in jail. He was released from prison after serving a sentence of only 11 months.

Nearly a year after his release from prison, Mehserle appealed his conviction to the First District Court of Appeals in San Francisco. His lawyer stated the purpose of this appeal was to allow Mehserle to return to "police work" which was not possible with this conviction on his record. They intended to continue to the state and the U.S. Supreme Court, fortunately the California Supreme Court unanimously denied review of an appellate ruling upholding the conviction.

The fact that Mehserle spent less than a year in prison is already an affront to justice, but it's one I could tolerate if he understood how/why he fucked up and realized/accepted that he shouldn't ever be in position of authority again. However the reasoning for his attempted appeals also shows him to believe that he should be allowed to return to "police work" after what he did, Which smacks of narcissism and is at best the sign of an irresponsible fool or at worst an unrepentant sociopath.

I'm not saying Oscar Grant was a model citizen but he did not deserve to die at the hands of man who is either grossly incompetent or a fucking murderer, and Officer Johannes Mehserle still hasn't paid even 1/10th the price he deserves to.
